claim: Macaque monkeys are widely used to study vision.
source: Macaque monkeys are widely used to study vision.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and introduction as established practice in the field.

claim: In the traditional approach, monkeys are brought into a lab to perform visual tasks while they are restrained to obtain stable eye tracking and neural recordings.
source: In the traditional approach, monkeys are brought into a lab to perform visual tasks while they are restrained to obtain stable eye tracking and neural recordings.
evidence: This describes the traditional methodology as background context.

claim: The authors designed a naturalistic environment with an integrated touchscreen workstation that enables high-quality eye tracking in unrestrained monkeys.
source: We designed a naturalistic environment with an integrated touchscreen workstation that enables high-quality eye tracking in unrestrained monkeys.
evidence: This is a primary claim about the study's methodology, supported by detailed descriptions and figures throughout the manuscript.

claim: Two naive monkeys were able to learn a complex same-different task through a combination of socially observing trained monkeys and solo trial-and-error.
source: As proof of concept, we show that two naive monkeys were able to learn this complex task through a combination of socially observing trained monkeys and solo trial-and-error.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and analysis presented in Figure 4 and related text.

claim: Macaque monkeys are highly intelligent and social animals with many similarities to humans.
source: Macaque monkeys are highly intelligent and social animals with many similarities to humans, due to which they are widely used to understand cognition and its neural basis (Passingham, 2009; Roelfsema and Treue, 2014; Buffalo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The traditional approach for studying vision prevents a deeper understanding of vision in more natural, unrestrained settings.
source: This approach prevents a deeper understanding of vision in more natural, unrestrained settings.
evidence: This is a reasoning-based claim about limitations of traditional methods.

claim: The design principles for naturalistic environments as well as standard procedures to maximize animal welfare are well understood.
source: The design principles for such naturalistic environments as well as standard procedures to maximize animal welfare are well understood now (Woolverton et al., 1989; Röder and Timmermans, 2002; Honess and Marin, 2006; Seier et al., 2011; Cannon et al., 2016; Coleman and Novak, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Recent studies have demonstrated that monkeys can be trained to perform complex tasks using touchscreen devices that can be easily integrated into a naturalistic environment.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that monkeys can be trained to perform complex tasks using touchscreen devices that can be easily integrated into a naturalistic environment (Rumbaugh et al., 1989; Mandell and Sackett, 2008; Fagot and Paleressompoulle, 2009; Gazes et al., 2013; Calapai et al., 2017; Claidière et al., 2017; Tulip et al., 2017; Berger et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: All commercial eye trackers work best when the head is in a stereotypical front-facing position with relatively little movement.
source: All commercial eye trackers work best when the head is in a stereotypical front-facing position with relatively little movement, and their gaze tracking degrades with any head movement.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of commercial eye tracking systems.

claim: Obtaining accurate gaze signals from unrestrained animals can be a major challenge.
source: As a result, obtaining accurate gaze signals from unrestrained animals can be a major challenge (for a review of existing literature and best practices, see Hopper et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Most studies of macaque eye tracking require some form of head restraint while monkeys are seated in a monkey chair.
source: Most studies of macaque eye tracking require some form of head restraint while monkeys are seated in a monkey chair (Machado and Nelson, 2011; De Luna and Rainer, 2014; Kawaguchi et al., 2019; Ryan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Wearable eye trackers require extensive animal training to avoid equipment damage.
source: Another solution is to use wearable eye trackers, but these require extensive animal training to avoid equipment damage (Milton et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Most eye trackers are optimized for larger screen distances (~60 cm) which allow for shallow angles between the eye tracker line-of-sight and the screen.
source: A further complication is that most eye trackers are optimized for larger screen distances (~60 cm) which allow for shallow angles between the eye tracker line-of-sight and the screen (Hopper et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: A macaque monkey reaching for a touchscreen requires far smaller distances (~20 cm), resulting in elevated angles for the eye tracker, which compromise tracking quality.
source: By contrast, a macaque monkey reaching for a touchscreen requires far smaller distances (~20 cm), resulting in elevated angles for the eye tracker, all of which compromise tracking quality.
evidence: This is an inference based on the geometric constraints of the setup.

claim: Many commercial eye-tracking systems are optimized for the human inter-pupillary distance (~60 mm) as opposed to that of monkeys (~30 mm), which result in compromised gaze tracking ability.
source: Finally, many commercial eye-tracking systems are optimized for the human inter-pupillary distance (~60 mm) as opposed to that of monkeys (~30 mm), which also result in compromised gaze tracking ability.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of commercial systems.

claim: The authors' custom-designed juice spout with a chin-rest brought the monkey into a stereotyped head position every time it drank juice.
source: This was possible due to a custom-designed juice spout with a chin-rest that brought the monkey into a stereotyped head position every time it drank juice, and by adjusting the eye tracker illuminator and camera positions
evidence: This is a description of the technical innovation that enabled high-quality eye tracking.

claim: The environment enables gaze-contingent tasks and high-fidelity eye tracking.
source: We show that this enables gaze-contingent tasks and high-fidelity eye tracking, both of which are crucial requirements for studying visual cognition.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Figure 3 and related analyses.

claim: The environment can be used to train monkeys on a complex same-different task by taking them through a sequence of subtasks of increasing complexity.
source: We show that this environment can be used to train monkeys on a complex same-different task by taking them through a sequence of subtasks of increasing complexity.
evidence: This is supported by the description of the Tailored Automated Training (TAT) paradigm and training outcomes.

claim: Naive monkeys can rapidly learn a complex task through a combination of socially observing trained monkeys perform the task at close quarters, and through solo sessions with trial-and-error learning.
source: Specifically, we show that naive monkeys can rapidly learn a complex task through a combination of socially observing trained monkeys perform the task at close quarters, and through solo sessions with trial-and-error learning.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from monkeys M2 and M4 presented in Figure 4 and supplements.

claim: Monkeys were group-housed in an enriched living environment with access to a touchscreen workstation where they could perform cognitive tasks for juice reward.
source: Monkeys were group-housed in an enriched living environment with access to a touchscreen workstation where they could perform cognitive tasks for juice reward (Figure 1A; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup, supported by Figure 1.

claim: The enriched environment comprised log perches and dead trees with natural as well as artificial lighting with several CCTV cameras to monitor movements.
source: The enriched environment comprised log perches and dead trees with natural as well as artificial lighting with several CCTV cameras to monitor movements (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the physical environment, supported by Figure 1B.

claim: The continuous camera recordings enabled reconstruction of activity maps of the animals with and without human interactions.
source: The continuous camera recordings enabled us to reconstruct activity maps of the animals with and without human interactions (Figure 1D; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by the activity maps shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The behavior room contained copper-sandwiched high pressure laminated panels that formed a closed circuit for removing external electromagnetic noise, to facilitate eventual brain recordings.
source: The behavior room contained copper-sandwiched high pressure laminated panels that formed a closed circuit for removing external electromagnetic noise, to facilitate eventual brain recordings (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a description of the electromagnetic shielding, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The entire workflow was designed so that experimenters would never have to directly handle or contact the animals during training.
source: The entire workflow was designed so that experimenters would never have to directly handle or contact the animals during training.
evidence: This is a description of the design principle for animal welfare.

claim: The authors were able to develop standard protocols to isolate each monkey and give it access to the behaviour room.
source: Even though the environment contained safe perches out of reach from humans, we were able to develop standard protocols to isolate each monkey and give it access to the behaviour room (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by the description in Materials and methods.

claim: Monkeys were trained to sit comfortably at the juice spout and perform tasks on the touchscreen for juice reward.
source: Monkeys were trained to sit comfortably at the juice spout and perform tasks on the touchscreen for juice reward.
evidence: This is a description of the training procedure.

claim: The juice delivery arm with a drain pipe ensured that monkeys drank juice directly from the juice spout after a correct trial instead of accessing spillover juice.
source: This was done to ensure that monkeys drank juice directly from the juice spout after a correct trial instead of subverting it and accessing spillover juice.
evidence: This is a description of the design rationale for the juice delivery system.

claim: The authors developed several modular head frames that were tailored to the typical shape of the monkey head.
source: Second, we developed several modular head frames that were tailored to the typical shape of the monkey head (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Monkeys comfortably rested their chin/head on the head frames and were willing to perform hundreds of trials even while using the most restrictive frames.
source: In practice, monkeys comfortably rested their chin/head on these frames and were willing to perform hundreds of trials even while using the most restrictive frames.
evidence: This is an observation from the training sessions.

claim: The removable hand grill was critical for reducing movement variability and providing an uninterrupted path for the light from the IR illuminator.
source: This was critical not only for reducing movement variability but also to provide an uninterrupted path for the light from the IR illuminator of the eye tracker mounted below the touchscreen to reflect off the eyes and reach the eye tracker camera mounted above the touch screen (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is a description of the design rationale, supported by Figure 2.

claim: The design essentially stereotyped the position of the monkey's head and gave excellent pupil and eye images and consequently highly accurate eye tracking.
source: This design essentially stereotyped the position of the monkey's head and gave us excellent pupil and eye images (Figure 2C, inset) and consequently highly accurate eye tracking (see Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2C inset and Video 2.

claim: Two animals (M1 & M3) were trained on a same-different (delayed match-to-sample) task with real-time gaze-contingency.
source: As a proof of concept, we trained two animals (M1 & M3) on a same-different (i.e., delayed match-to-sample) task with real-time gaze-contingency.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The monkey had to keep its hand on the hold cue and maintain its gaze within a 8° radius around the fixation cross.
source: The monkey had to keep its hand on the hold cue and maintain its gaze within a 8° radius around the fixation cross.
evidence: This is a description of the task requirements.

claim: The sample image appeared for 500 ms after which the screen went blank for 200 ms.
source: Following this a sample image appeared for 500 ms after which the screen went blank for 200 ms.
evidence: This is a description of the task timing.

claim: The animal had to make a response by touching one of the choice buttons within 5 s.
source: The animal had to make a response by touching one of the choice buttons within 5 s.
evidence: This is a description of the task requirements.

claim: Highly reliable gaze position was obtained across trials.
source: We obtained highly reliable gaze position across trials (Figure 3E), allowing us to reconstruct the characteristic time course of saccades (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3E-G showing consistent gaze patterns.

claim: The accuracy of eye tracking is remarkable given that this is from entirely unrestrained monkeys.
source: This accuracy is remarkable given that this is from entirely unrestrained monkeys.
evidence: This is an evaluative statement based on the data presented.

claim: Similar, highly reliable gaze signals were obtained from another animal M3.
source: We obtained similar, highly reliable gaze signals from another animal M3 as well (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gaze data was missing if and only if the animal looked away or moved away from the touchscreen, with no gaze data lost when the monkeys did not look away.
source: By comparing our networked video cameras with the eye tracker gaze position signals, we found that gaze data was missing if and only if the animal looked away or moved away from the touchscreen, with no gaze data lost when the monkeys did not look away.
evidence: This is based on comparison of video and eye tracking data.

claim: Although a relatively liberal fixation window (radius = 8°) was imposed, the animals' eye positions were far more concentrated within a given trial with average gaze position changing slightly from trial to trial.
source: Although we imposed a relatively liberal fixation window (radius = 8°), the animals' eye positions were far more concentrated within a given trial with average gaze position changing slightly from trial to trial (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3H showing gaze positions.

claim: Gaze was tightly centered with a small standard deviation (standard deviation, mean ± s.d. across 150 trials: 0.90° ± 0.36° along x, 1.01° ± 0.38° along y).
source: This revealed gaze to be tightly centered with a small standard deviation (standard deviation, mean ± s.d. across 150 trials: 0.90° ± 0.36° along x, 1.01° ± 0.38° along y).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of fixation quality from the data.

claim: Similar tightly centered standard deviation was obtained across sessions.
source: We obtained similar, tightly centered standard deviation across sessions (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3J.

claim: The eye tracking revealed that monkey M3 looked first at the DIFFERENT button by default and then made a corrective saccade to the SAME button.
source: Interestingly, the eye tracking revealed that monkey M3 looked first at the DIFFERENT button by default and then made a corrective saccade to the SAME button (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the eye tracking data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both monkeys M1 and M3 were trained on a fixation task and highly accurate eye tracking and fixation quality were obtained in both monkeys.
source: Finally, we also trained both monkeys M1 and M3 on a fixation task and obtained highly accurate eye tracking and fixation quality in both monkeys (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The high fidelity of gaze data in unrestrained monkeys was due to the stereotyped position of the juice spout and the split placement of the eye tracker camera and IR illuminator.
source: This high fidelity of gaze data in unrestrained monkeys was due to two crucial innovations. First, the stereotyped position of the juice spout made the animal put its head in exactly the same position each time, enabling accurate eye tracking (Video 2). Second, the eye tracker camera and IR illuminator were split and placed above and below the screen, enabling high-quality pupil and corneal reflections, boosting tracking fidelity.
evidence: This is an explanation of the technical factors contributing to high-quality eye tracking.

claim: In the traditional paradigm, before any task training can be started, monkeys have to be gradually acclimatized to entering specialized monkey chairs and to having their head immobilized using headposts for eye tracking, which can take a few months.
source: In the traditional paradigm, before any task training can be started, monkeys have to be gradually acclimatized to entering specialized monkey chairs that block them from access to their head, and to having their head immobilized using headposts for the purpose of eye tracking. This process can take a few months and therefore is a major bottleneck in training (Fernström et al., 2009; Slater et al., 2016; Mason et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: These steps are no longer required in the authors' environment, allowing focus entirely on task-relevant training.
source: These steps are no longer required in our environment, allowing us to focus entirely on task-relevant training.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantage of the new environment.

claim: Two monkeys (M1 and M3) were trained using Tailored Automated Training (TAT).
source: We trained two monkeys (M1 and M3) using TAT (for details, see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a description of the training procedure.

claim: Each monkey went through a unique trajectory of learning that was tailored to its competence on each stage.
source: Importantly, each monkey went through a unique trajectory of learning that was tailored to its competence on each stage.
evidence: This is a description of the TAT approach.

claim: There were a total of 10 stages and multiple levels within each stage in the TAT paradigm.
source: There were a total of 10 stages and multiple levels within each stage.
evidence: This is a description of the TAT structure.

claim: Only one task-related parameter was varied across levels in any given stage.
source: Only one task-related parameter was varied across levels in any given stage.
evidence: This is a description of the TAT design principle.

claim: The monkey would progress to the next level once it completed most recent 50 trials with at least 80% accuracy.
source: The monkey would progress to the next level once it completed most recent 50 trials with at least 80% accuracy.
evidence: This is a description of the progression criterion in TAT.

claim: By the end of training, both monkeys were highly accurate on the same-different task (91% for M1, 82% for M3).
source: By the end of training, both monkeys were highly accurate on the same-different task (91% for M1, 82% for M3).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of training outcome.

claim: The duration of training from completely naïve to fully trained was approximately 90 sessions or days.
source: The duration of training from completely naïve to fully trained was approximately 90 sessions or days.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of training duration.

claim: The tailored automated training (TAT) paradigm deployed in this naturalistic environment can enable automated training of monkeys on complex cognitive tasks while maximizing animal welfare.
source: Thus, the tailored automated training (TAT) paradigm deployed in this naturalistic environment can enable automated training of monkeys on complex cognitive tasks while at the same time maximizing animal welfare.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the training results.

claim: Social learning experiments were performed on two naïve monkeys (M2 and M4).
source: To explore this possibility, we performed social learning experiments on two naïve monkeys (M2 and M4).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: In each case, the naïve monkey was introduced along with a trained monkey (M1/M3) into the behaviour room, giving it the opportunity to learn by observation.
source: In each case, the naïve monkey was introduced along with a trained monkey (M1/M3) into the behaviour room, giving it the opportunity to learn by observation.
evidence: This is a description of the social learning procedure.

claim: For monkey M2, each day of social training involved three sessions: first with M1, then with M3, and finally a solo session.
source: Each day of social training for M2 involved three sessions in which he was first introduced into the behaviour room along with M1, then introduced together with M3, and finally a solo session.
evidence: This is a description of the training schedule.

claim: For M4 social training, a social session with M3 and a solo session were included.
source: For M4 social training, we included a social session with M3 and a solo session.
evidence: This is a description of the training schedule.

claim: Neither monkey M2 nor M4 was acquainted with the setup at all prior to social training.
source: Neither monkey was acquainted with the setup at all prior to this.
evidence: This is a description of the initial conditions.

claim: Naive monkey M2 was intermediate in its social rank, with trained monkey M1 being higher and M3 being lower in rank.
source: Here, naive monkey (M2) was intermediate in its social rank, with one of the trained monkeys (M1) being higher and the other (M3) being lower in rank.
evidence: This is a description of the social hierarchy.

claim: CCTV footage was used to retrospectively identify which monkey was doing the task on each trial during the social sessions.
source: We used CCTV footage to retrospectively identify which monkey was doing the task on each trial during the social sessions.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method.

claim: On Day 1, M1 intimidated M2 and prevented any access to the workstation, and M2 did the same to M3.
source: On Day 1, we observed interactions expected from the social hierarchy: M1 intimidated M2 and prevented any access to the workstation, and M2 did the same to M3.
evidence: This is an observation from the video data.

claim: The M1-M2 dynamic remained like this throughout the social sessions.
source: The M1-M2 dynamic remained like this throughout the social sessions.
evidence: This is an observation from the video data.

claim: On Day 4, M2 pulled M3 into the behaviour room, and a few trials were observed in which M2 drank juice while M3 performed a few correct trials.
source: On Day 4, M2 pulled M3 into the behaviour room, and we observed a few trials in which M2 drank juice while M3 performed a few correct trials.
evidence: This is an observation from the video data.

claim: By Day 5, M2 was observing M1 closely in the M1-M2 social sessions, and began to slide his hand to make a response in the M2-M3 social sessions.
source: By Day 5, M2 was observing M1 closely in the M1-M2 social sessions, and began to slide his hand to make a response in the M2-M3 social sessions.
evidence: This is an observation from the video data.

claim: By Day 9, M2 was performing the task at chance level.
source: By Day 9, M2 was performing the task at chance level.
evidence: This is based on behavioral performance data.

claim: By Day 13, there were no interactions between M1 and M2 and no interactions between M2 and M3.
source: By Day 13, there were no interactions between M1 and M2 (with M1 dominating throughout) and no interactions between M2 and M3 (with M2 dominating throughout).
evidence: This is an observation from the video data.

claim: From Day 13 onwards, M2 was introduced by himself into the behaviour room and took eight more sessions to reach above-chance accuracy on the task.
source: We therefore stopped the social sessions and began introducing M2 by himself into the behaviour room. From here on, M2 took eight more sessions to reach above-chance accuracy on the task.
evidence: This is based on behavioral performance data.

claim: By the end of 29 sessions, M2 had achieved 91% accuracy on the task.
source: By the end of 29 sessions, M2 had achieved 91 % accuracy on the task.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of training outcome.

claim: Monkey M2 began to initiate trials correctly and make choice responses by Day 5, and his performance began to rise above chance by about Day 15.
source: It can be seen that monkey M2 began to initiate trials correctly and make choice responses by Day 5, and his performance began to rise above chance by about Day 15.
evidence: This is based on analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: M2 began to increase his second chance accuracy almost immediately after introducing immediate repeat of error on Day 10.
source: This revealed an interesting pattern, whereby M2 began to increase his second chance accuracy, presumably by switching his response upon making an error almost immediately after introducing immediate repeat of error on Day 10 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: M2's first-chance accuracy only began to increase a few days later, from Day 16 onwards.
source: Interestingly his first-chance accuracy only began to increase a few days later, from Day 16 onwards (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: M2 learned to touch by Day 2, respond to choice buttons by about Day 5, and began to make correct responses significantly above chance by Day 15.
source: The resulting plot (Figure 4C), shows that M2 learned to touch by Day 2, respond to choice buttons by about Day 5, and began to make correct responses significantly above chance by Day 15.
evidence: This is based on analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The naïve monkey M4 was socially dominant over the trained monkey M3 at the start.
source: Since we observed more interactions between M2 and M3 during social learning of M2, we selected the naïve monkey (M4) to be socially dominant over the trained monkey (M3).
evidence: This is a description of the initial social hierarchy.

claim: The social dominance between M4 and M3 reversed over time so that M3 became dominant over M4 by the start of the social sessions, and this trend also reversed at times across sessions.
source: However, this social dominance reversed over time so that M3 became dominant over M4 by the start of the social sessions, and this trend also reversed at times across sessions.
evidence: This is an observation from the video data.

claim: For M4, each day of social learning consisted of three sessions: a solo session with only M3 performing the task, followed by a social session where M4 was introduced with M3, and finally a solo session with only M4.
source: On each day of social learning, we conducted three sessions: a solo session with only M3 performing the task, followed by a social session where M4 was introduced into the room with M3 already present, and finally a solo session with only M4.
evidence: This is a description of the training schedule.

claim: M4 learned to touch correctly by Day 2, began to touch the choice buttons by Day 5, and his accuracy increased steadily thereafter reflecting continuous learning.
source: To summarize, M4 learned to touch correctly by Day 2, began to touch the choice buttons by Day five and his accuracy increased steadily thereafter reflecting continuous learning (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A post-hoc analysis revealed that M4's improvement was primarily due to increase in second-chance accuracy with little or no change in first-chance accuracy.
source: However, a post-hoc analysis revealed that this improvement was primarily due to increase in second-chance accuracy with little or no change in first-chance accuracy.
evidence: This is based on analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Monkey M4 demonstrated an initial phase of learning task structure, followed by a later stage of trial-and-error learning similar to monkey M2.
source: Thus, monkey M4 also demonstrated an initial phase of learning task structure, followed by a later stage of trial-and-error learning similar to the monkey M2.
evidence: This is a comparison of learning patterns between M2 and M4.

claim: The learning curve for M4 was unlike that seen for M2.
source: However the learning curve for M4 was unlike that seen for M2.
evidence: This is a comparison of learning patterns.

claim: M2 learned the same-different rule while also learning to switch his response on immediate-repeat trials, whereas M4 only learned the suboptimal rule of switching his response on immediate-repeat trials.
source: Whereas M2 learned the same-different rule while also learning to switch his response on immediate-repeat trials, M4 only learned the suboptimal rule of switching his response on immediate-repeat trials.
evidence: This is a comparison of learning outcomes between M2 and M4.

claim: M4 was successful at trial-and-error learning on this task, albeit with suboptimal learning.
source: Nonetheless, M4 was successful at trial-and-error learning on this task, albeit with suboptimal learning.
evidence: This is an evaluation of M4's learning outcome.

claim: Both naïve monkeys (M2 and M4) learned the task in two distinct phases.
source: The above observations demonstrate that both naïve monkeys (M2 and M4) learned the task in two distinct phases.
evidence: This is a summary of the learning patterns observed.

claim: In the first phase, the naïve monkeys learned the basic structure of the task through social interactions and learning.
source: In the first phase, they learned the basic structure of the task through social interactions and learning.
evidence: This is a characterization of the first learning phase.

claim: By task structure, the authors mean the specific sequence of actions that the animal has to perform to receive reward at chance levels.
source: By task structure we mean the specific sequence of actions that the animal has to perform to receive reward at chance levels: here, these actions involve holding one button until the test image appears and then touching one of the choice buttons afterwards and removing his hand from the touchscreen to initiate the next trial.
evidence: This is a definition provided by the authors.

claim: The first stage of learning took only a few days during social learning.
source: This stage took only a few days during social learning.
evidence: This is based on the timeline of behavioral data.

claim: By the end of the first stage, both monkeys did not seem to be benefiting from socially observing or interacting with the trained monkey.
source: By the end of this stage, both monkeys did not seem to be benefiting from socially observing or interacting with the trained monkey.
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data.

claim: In the second phase, M2 learned the same-different rule all by himself through trial-and-error, by improving on both his first-chance and second-chance accuracy.
source: In the second phase, M2 learned the same-different rule all by himself through trial-and-error, by improving on both his first-chance and second-chance accuracy.
evidence: This is based on analysis of behavioral data.

claim: M4 showed learning on the task but his improvement was driven by his second-chance accuracy alone, indicating that he learned a suboptimal rule to improve his task performance.
source: M4 also showed learning on the task but unlike M2, his improvement was driven by his second-chance accuracy alone, indicating that he learned a suboptimal rule to improve his task performance.
evidence: This is based on analysis of behavioral data.

claim: In both monkeys, the social sessions naturally dissociated these two stages of learning.
source: Nonetheless, in both monkeys, the social sessions naturally dissociated these two stages of learning.
evidence: This is a summary of the learning patterns observed.

claim: The novel naturalistic environment with a touchscreen workstation with high-quality eye tracking can be used to study visual cognition as well as natural and social behaviors in unrestrained monkeys.
source: Here, we designed a novel naturalistic environment with a touchscreen workstation with high-quality eye tracking that can be used to study visual cognition as well as natural and social behaviors in unrestrained monkeys.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: High-quality eye tracking can be achieved in unrestrained, freely moving monkeys working at the touchscreen on a complex cognitive task.
source: First, we show that high-quality eye tracking can be achieved in unrestrained, freely moving monkeys working at the touchscreen on a complex cognitive task.
evidence: This is a major outcome supported by data in Figure 3 and supplements.

claim: Interesting novel behaviors can be observed in this environment, specifically that two naïve monkeys were able to learn aspects of a complex cognitive task through a combination of socially observing trained monkeys doing the task and solo trial-and-error.
source: Second, we show that interesting novel behaviors can be observed in this environment: specifically, two naïve monkeys were able to learn aspects of a complex cognitive task through a combination of socially observing trained monkeys doing the task and solo trial-and-error.
evidence: This is a major outcome supported by data in Figure 4 and supplements.

claim: The novel naturalistic environment with a touchscreen is similar to other efforts where the common goal is a seamless behavior station to enable training monkeys within their living environment.
source: Our novel naturalistic environment with a touchscreen is similar to other efforts (Calapai et al., 2017; Tulip et al., 2017; Berger et al., 2018), where the common goal is a seamless behavior station to enable training monkeys within their living environment.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The authors were able to achieve precise monitoring of gaze in unrestrained macaque monkeys.
source: First, we were able to achieve precise monitoring of gaze in unrestrained macaque monkeys.
evidence: This is a claimed advantage of the new environment.

claim: While viable gaze tracking has been reported in unrestrained large animals, there are technical challenges in achieving this with unrestrained macaque monkeys, whose small size results in an elevated line of sight for any eye tracker placed at arm's length.
source: While viable gaze tracking has been reported in unrestrained large animals, there are technical challenges in achieving this with unrestrained macaque monkeys, whose small size results in an elevated line of sight for any eye tracker placed at arm's length.
evidence: This is a description of technical challenges.

claim: This is the first report of accurate eye tracking in unrestrained macaque monkeys interacting at close quarters with a touchscreen.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first report of accurate eye tracking in unrestrained macaque monkeys interacting at close quarters with a touchscreen.
evidence: This is a claim of novelty.

claim: Gaze signals are required for any complex cognitive tasks involving visual stimuli.

claim: Above and below the monitor on the behavior station were two acrylic window openings.

source: Acrylic also offered better mechanical strength and scratch resistance compared to polycarbonate.

source: Positioning their heads within the head restraint was not a challenge for the monkeys and they habituated to it within tens of trials.
evidence: This is an observation about animal behavior.

claim: The reward for performing the task correctly was provided to the monkey as juice drops delivered at the tip of a custom reward delivery arm.
source: The reward for performing the task correctly was provided to the monkey as juice drops delivered at the tip of a custom reward delivery arm (Figure 2A–B; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a description of the reward system.

source: This reward arm was a 1" width hollow square section stainless steel tube. Concealed within it are two thin stainless-steel pipes – a juice pipe for delivering the juice to the monkey and a drainpipe to collect any remaining juice dripping from the juice pipe.
evidence: This is a description of the reward arm design.

claim: The juice was delivered using a generic peristaltic pump on the pipe connecting the juice bottle to the end of the juice pipe in the control room.
source: The juice was delivered using a generic peristaltic pump on the pipe connecting the juice bottle to the end of the juice pipe in the control room.
evidence: This is a description of the juice delivery mechanism.

source: This pump was controlled by a custom voltage-dependent current driver circuit printed to a PCB (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) which in turn is controlled through a digital signal from NIMH MonkeyLogic via the DIOxBNC board.
evidence: This is a description of the control system.

claim: The reward arm was mounted on a linear guide which allowed adjustment of the distance of juice pipe tip and the touchscreen.
source: The reward arm was mounted on a linear guide which allowed us to adjust the distance of juice pipe tip (near monkeys' mouth) and the touchscreen.
evidence: This is a description of the design flexibility.

claim: As a result, the authors can passively ensure the monkey sat at a distance that enables it to give touch response without having to stretch their arms and gave a good field of view of the monkeys' face and body for the cameras.
source: As a result, we can passively ensure the monkey sat at a distance that enables it to give touch response without having to stretch their arms and gave a good field of view of the monkeys' face and body for the cameras.
evidence: This is a description of the design rationale.

source: Eye movements were recorded using a customized small form factor ETL 300HD eye tracker from ISCAN Inc, USA with optical lenses that enabled eye tracking at close quarters.

source: The eye-tracker primarily consisted of an infrared monochrome video capture system that we oriented to get a field of view that covered both eyes of the animal when its mouth was positioned at the juice spout and the animal was in position to do trials.
evidence: This is a description of the eye tracker setup.

source: We resolved this issue by splitting the relative positions of the IR illuminator (placing it below the touchscreen) and the IR sensitive camera (placed above the touchscreen; see Figure 2) of the eye tracker system to provide robust eye tracking across the range of eye movements within our task.
evidence: This is a description of the solution to the technical problem.

claim: The ISCAN system offers a parameterizable eye-gate, which is a rectangular aperture in the monochrome camera's field of view and restricts the search space of the pupil and eye-glint search routines in the ISCAN software algorithm.
source: The ISCAN system offers a parameterizable eye-gate, which is in effect a rectangular aperture in the monochrome camera's field of view and restricts the search space of the pupil and eye-glint search routines in the ISCAN software algorithm.
evidence: This is a description of the eye tracker software features.

claim: The pupil and eye-glint search are based on the area (minimum number of pixels) and intensity-based thresholds that can be manipulated using interactive sliders in ISCAN's DQW software.
source: The pupil and eye-glint search are based on the area (minimum number of pixels) and intensity-based thresholds that can be manipulated using interactive sliders in ISCAN's DQW software.
evidence: This is a description of the eye tracker software features.

claim: The authors modeled the raw eye-gaze signal as the horizontal and vertical signed difference between centroids of the detected pupil and eye-glint regions of interest.
source: We modeled the raw eye-gaze signal as the horizontal and vertical signed difference between centroids of the detected pupil and eye-glint regions of interest.
evidence: This is a description of the gaze calculation method.

claim: The raw eye signal was communicated in real time to the computer running NIMH ML through the DIOxBNC analog cables.
source: The raw eye signal was communicated in real time to the computer running NIMH ML through the DIOxBNC analog cables.
evidence: This is a description of the data communication system.

source: This raw eye-signal was read into the NIMH ML software and got rendered in real time onto another monitor that displayed a copy of the visual stimuli shown on the monkey touchscreen, while the monkeys performed touch-based visual tasks.
evidence: This is a description of the real-time visualization system.

source: We evaluated other commercial trackers but found limitations such as the need for semi-transparent hot mirror on the monkey side or a sticker to be affixed on the monkey forehead (EyeLink).
evidence: This is a description of limitations of other eye trackers.

source: Neither of these were practical options at the time of evaluation.
evidence: This is an evaluation of alternative options.

source: We also found that other trackers popular for non-human primate research (Tobii X-120, Tobii Pro Spectrum) did not work as reliably for our monkeys, presumably due to species differences.
evidence: This is a description of limitations of other eye trackers.

claim: Such species specific limitations of commercial eye trackers have been reported before.
source: Such species specific limitations of commercial eye trackers have been reported before (Hopper et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: NIMH ML has a feature to display visual cues at selected locations on a uniform grid that the monkey can either touch or look at and obtain the liquid reward.
source: NIMH ML has a feature to display visual cues at selected locations on a uniform grid that the monkey can either touch or look at and obtain the liquid reward.
evidence: This is a description of the software features.

claim: The authors trained their monkeys to look at and then touch these visual cues.
source: We trained our monkeys to look at and then touch these visual cues.
evidence: This is a description of the training procedure.

claim: Since monkeys typically make an eye movement while initiating and performing the reach and touch, the authors exploited this to first center the raw eye signal with respect to the center of the screen and subsequently obtain a coarse scaling factor between changes in the raw eye signal and corresponding changes in the on-screen location.
source: Since monkeys typically make an eye movement while initiating and performing the reach and touch, we exploited this to first center the raw eye signal with respect to the center of the screen and subsequently obtain a coarse scaling factor between changes in the raw eye signal and corresponding changes in the on-screen location.
evidence: This is a description of the calibration procedure.

claim: In this manner, the authors obtained a rough offset and scaling factor that maps the raw eye gaze signal with the on-screen locations of the monkey touch screen.
source: In this manner, we obtained a rough offset and scaling factor that maps the raw eye gaze signal with the on-screen locations of the monkey touch screen.
evidence: This is a description of the calibration outcome.

claim: The authors then ran calibration trials where four rectangular fixation cues were presented in random order, and the animal had to look at each fixation cue while maintaining hold on a button.
source: We then ran calibration trials where four rectangular fixation cues were presented in random order. The animal had to look at each fixation cue as and when it was shown, all the while maintaining hold on a button on the right extreme portion of the screen.
evidence: This is a description of the calibration procedure.

claim: The animal received a liquid reward at the end of a complete cycle of fixation cues for correctly maintaining fixation throughout the trials.
source: The animal received a liquid reward at the end of a complete cycle of fixation cues for correctly maintaining fixation throughout the trials.
evidence: This is a description of the reward contingency.

claim: These calibration trials provided pairs of raw eye-gaze (x, y) observations that corresponded to known locations on the touch screen.
source: These calibration trials provided us with pairs of raw eye-gaze (x, y) observations that corresponded to known locations on the touch screen.
evidence: This is a description of the calibration data.

claim: The authors used linear regression to learn a transformation between the raw eye-data to touchscreen positions.
source: We then used linear regression to learn a transformation between the raw eye-data to touchscreen positions.
evidence: This is a description of the calibration method.

claim: The authors used these session-wise calibration models to transform eye-data if a higher degree of accuracy was required than what is provided by the initial coarse offset and scaling of the eye-signal.
source: We used these session-wise calibration models to transform eye-data if a higher degree of accuracy was required than what is provided by the initial coarse offset and scaling of the eye-signal that we manually perform in the beginning of each trial.
evidence: This is a description of the calibration application.

claim: In practice, even the coarse centering and scaling of raw eye-data was sufficient for gaze-contingent paradigms where the monkeys had to either passively view successive stimuli in a fixation paradigm, or when they had to maintain gaze on the sample and test stimuli during the same-different tasks.
source: In practice, even the coarse centering and scaling of raw eye-data was sufficient for gaze-contingent paradigms where the monkeys had to either passively view successive stimuli in a fixation paradigm, or when they had to maintain gaze on the sample and test stimuli during the same-different tasks.
evidence: This is an observation about the calibration accuracy.

claim: Although linear regression was sufficient for the authors' purposes, biquadratic transformations might further improve gaze quality.
source: Although linear regression was sufficient for our purposes, we note that biquadratic transformations might further improve gaze quality (Kimmel et al., 2012; Bozomitu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a suggestion for potential improvement, supported by citations.

claim: The authors performed a motion heatmap analysis on the CCTV videos recorded from the play area using publicly available code.
source: We performed a motion heatmap analysis on the CCTV videos recorded from the play area using publicly available code (https://github.com/andikarachman/Motion-Heatmap; Rachman, 2019; copy available at our OSF data/code repository ).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: This analysis was helpful to visualize movement patterns over time and is performed frame by frame.
source: This analysis was helpful to visualize movement patterns over time and is performed frame by frame.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis purpose.

claim: On each frame, the background image is subtracted and thresholded to remove small motion signals, the result is added to the accumulation image, and a colour map is applied and overlayed on the background image to obtain the final output.
source: On each frame, the background image is subtracted and thresholded to remove small motion signals. The result of the threshold is added to the accumulation image, and a colour map is applied. The colour map is overlayed on the background image to obtain the final output.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis algorithm.

claim: Previous efforts have used color markers for activity and movement analyses.
source: We note that previous efforts have used color markers for activity and movement analyses (Ballesta et al., 2014), and more recently it has become possible to use markerless movement and pose tracking (Mathis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior methods, supported by citations.

claim: More recently it has become possible to use markerless movement and pose tracking.
source: We note that previous efforts have used color markers for activity and movement analyses (Ballesta et al., 2014), and more recently it has become possible to use markerless movement and pose tracking (Mathis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of recent advances, supported by a citation.

claim: The authors quantified the consistency of the mean gaze fixation during periods of fixation contingent behavior by plotting the relative probability of the mean fixations across trials in each session for each monkey.
source: We quantified the consistency of the mean gaze fixation during periods of fixation contingent behavior by plotting the relative probability of the mean fixations (within a trial) across trials in each session for each monkey.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

source: Briefly, we calibrated the raw eye-data using the calibration models built with data from calibration trials and segregated the data during the period of fixation contingency (from initial fixation acquisition to after inter stimulus interval or end of trial, for same-different and fixation tasks respectively).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing steps.

claim: The authors took the mean fixation location within a trial and plotted the relative probability of the mean fixations across all trials in the session using the histogram2 function in MATLAB.
source: We took the mean fixation location within a trial and plotted the relative probability of the mean fixations across all trials in the session using the histogram2 function provided in MATLAB with the normalization property set to 'probability'.
evidence: This is a description of the visualization method.

claim: Violin plots were based on code from Holger Hoffmann's Violin Plot programs.
source: Violin plots were based on code from Holger Hoffmann's Violin Plot programs (retrieved on June 30, 2021 from MATLAB Central File Exchange https://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/45134-violin-plot).
